## TL;DR

Task cards and the task drawer now recognize checks from three server-owned signals: persisted handoff status, recorded check runs, and a live local check slot held for that task. A reload during a CLI-requested handoff can therefore show the active step and elapsed time even if the check-run list is empty. While RepoOS owns the check, the card and drawer avoid treating the engineer's silence as a stall. The task drawer shows the active progress bar in its status region; the obsolete disabled copy in the action area has been removed. Preview screenshots use client-only fixture data without requesting nonexistent task records.

## Work and rationale

The original report described a mismatch between server state and the UI's evidence. `repoos handoff-status` reads the persisted handoff status, but the UI previously depended on live handoff SSE or a running `handoff-finalize` row in check history. The latter is not guaranteed because some handoff callers run checks without the optional task-check instrumentation. The server status is therefore the durable ownership signal, with check history retained as a richer source of progress when present.

The store hydrates and polls persisted handoff status. Active cards fetch it when mounted, then continue polling only when it reports a running handoff. The drawer refreshes status with its existing check loop. Handoff check progress markers are persisted with the status, so the card and drawer can recover step, timing, test-file progress, attempt, and machine after reload. The same data feeds the progress bar above the task drawer tabs; indeterminate progress keeps a readable label without inventing a percentage.

Round-one screenshot verification exposed another fixture boundary: opening the seeded #9999 drawer caused status and summary requests to reach the preview API, which correctly returned 404 because #9999 exists only in client fixture state. The store now skips handoff-status and check-history requests for that captured fixture, and the drawer skips task-summary requests. A regression test verifies that the handoff and check hydration paths make no request for the seeded fixture. This preserves realistic API behavior while keeping preview capture free of expected missing-task errors.

The automated review also identified a second way for the UI to miss a running check: the task can hold a local check slot while the task-check run list is empty. The store now reads the existing `/api/local-check-slots` endpoint, coalesces concurrent requests, and caches the snapshot briefly so many active cards do not fan out duplicate requests. It identifies a live holder by its local-check metadata and task id, ignores dead holders, and advances elapsed time from the server-reported slot age. Both card and drawer treat that holder as running check work and use its age for the status label. The drawer refreshes slot ownership with its existing polling loop; active cards hydrate it on mount. This state takes priority over agent-silence repair hints.

The drawer previously contained two progress-bar blocks: the active status-region bar and an older block hidden behind `false && inPipeline && activeCheckRun`. I removed the dead copy so there is one live status-region implementation and one test selector. The review described this as a TaskDrawer merge conflict; inspection found no unresolved Git conflict markers, and the practical conflict was the obsolete duplicate competing with the restored status-card progress bar.

## Approaches tried

Initially the card and drawer relied on live events plus check history. That reproduced the reload problem when a CLI requested handoff and the run list was empty. I then wired the UI to persisted handoff status and kept check rows for detailed progress. An initial polling approach attached timers to every active card; existing board-budget coverage rejected that. The final handoff approach fetches status on mount and polls only while status is running.

For locally held checks, I considered using the resource queue marker, but those markers represent waiters, not slot owners. The Checks page already obtains holder metadata from `/api/local-check-slots`, including PID, task id, age, heartbeat age, and whether the process is dead. Reusing that API supplies the required ownership signal without changing the server's slot format or inferring a running check from a queued marker.

## Challenges and blockers

The first handoff after the main UI work failed because its screenshot route did not open the drawer. Updating the declared route fixed the missing-target issue. The next capture then exposed real API requests caused by the client-only fixture; I added scoped fetch guards and verified the complete screenshot and UI gate. An earlier finalization attempt exceeded the server deadline while its remote full gate was still running. A manually invoked full check subsequently passed, and later review verification completed successfully.

During review round one, the findings were initially broad: resolve the TaskDrawer progress duplication, account for held local slots, and remove the disabled duplicate bar. I inspected the reviewed worktree, confirmed it had no unresolved conflict markers, and resolved the actionable overlap by deleting the obsolete action-area block while preserving the live bar above the tabs. The new local-slot state and card/drawer regression coverage passed the full check.

## Key learnings

A check-run list is a history view, not a complete ownership registry. Handoff status covers RepoOS-owned finalization; a local slot covers checks executing without a recorded task run. Queue markers answer a different question: whether a task is waiting for a slot. Keeping those signals separate prevents both false “paused” states and false claims that a waiting task is already running.

Preview fixtures also need guards at every task-specific API boundary they exercise. A fixture can render correctly yet fail verification because a secondary polling request treats its synthetic id as real. Finally, duplicate UI paths become maintenance hazards even when one is disabled: tests and reviewers may target the old selector while the visible interface uses a newer component. Removing the obsolete block leaves a single source of truth for check progress.
